fatal_errors: The proposed aging intervention does not reconstruct the high-energy ball milling plus spark-plasma-sintering comparison central to the target.
The cited evidence does not demonstrate facile dislocation glide, enhanced dynamic recovery, low work hardening, or precipitate-controlled strengthening.

The evidence reports substantial strength and hardness in single-phase FCC CoCrFeNiTix materials, so it does not substantiate the premise that an FCC state intrinsically causes low hardness and strength.

The falsification rule confounds failure of the mechanism with failure of the aging treatment to generate precipitates; absence of precipitates cannot test whether dynamic recovery governs the starting state.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the requested property tradeoff and proposes a controlled untreated-versus-aged comparison with mechanical testing and TEM, so it has reasonable problem alignment and some experimental testability. However, it misses the target intervention, processing conditions, nanocrystalline FCC/BCC structural mediator, and the combined Hall–Petch, milling-induced dislocation, and solid-solution strengthening mechanism. It also omits the target quantitative outcomes of approximately 675 HV, 1894 MPa compressive strength, 1238 MPa yield stress, high density, and intergranular fracture. Its baseline overlaps only generally with an as-cast comparison and does not account for porosity or microstructural heterogeneity. Most importantly, E1 supports neither dynamic recovery nor easy slip as the cause of low strength. A valid discriminating test would directly compare recovery and dislocation mobility in otherwise matched microstructures, rather than infer the starting-state mechanism merely from whether an aging treatment strengthens the alloy.
